article_text:
T o direct one movie that is on everyone’s lips in awards season is remarkable. To make two begins to look like sorcery. That is the position in which the 30-year-old Florida-born film-maker Lance Oppenheim now finds himself. Next month brings the release of You Can See Everything , the three-hour documentary which he co-directed with faux-naif deadpan imp Nathan Fielder, in which they spend a month living with the disgraced health-tech mogul Elizabeth Holmes before she begins her 11-year prison sentence for fraud and conspiracy. The film, described by Oppenheim as “head-spinning” and so shrouded in secrecy that Variety magazine’s list of Oscar predictions identifies one of its cast members only as “[Redacted]”, is expected to become the first documentary nominated for best picture.

When I meet Oppenheim in a London hotel, it is to discuss his other hot ticket, Primetime, for which Robert Pattinson is the one attracting Oscar buzz. The Batman actor gives a high-wire performance as Chris Hansen, the sensationalist US television vigilante renowned for ambushing paedophiles on To Catch a Predator, which was a disreputable and highly addictive segment of the current affairs show Dateline NBC between 2004 and 2007. Hansen later parlayed the idea, and his crusading shtick, into a succession of spin-offs. Some, including Hansen Vs Predators, had the same sleazy catnip quality. Others, such as a sting to collar bicycle thieves, did not.

The format of To Catch a Predator is simple. A volunteer from the website Perverted-Justice enters an online chatroom pretending to be underage. Once a paedophile takes the bait, chats with the supposed teen and then pitches up at the agreed location (which is in fact a “sting house” rigged with cameras), he is met by an actor posing as the adolescent. Suddenly, Hansen slinks out of the shadows and calmly invites the offender to “have a seat,” an offer which quickly became his catchphrase. He then reads aloud excerpts from the incriminating online chat as the guilty party squirms and panics. Reality television this may be, but it is also a theatrical performance with its own unvarying props from one sting to the next: cookies and pizza the pre-sex snacks, a table or kitchen island Hansen’s equivalent of a CEO’s desk or judge’s bench.

“The show is so tonally strange,” marvels Oppenheim. “It feels like an alien object beamed in from Mars. You’re seeing this horrific situation where someone who’s sick in the head has shown up to do a terrible thing. Then they’re confronted by Chris Hansen, who has these catchphrases and one-liners. He’s a crime-stopper but he’s also there to make a TV show out of their miserable state. It oscillated between making me nauseated and making me laugh. The challenge for me was how to create something that’s even stranger than stranger-than-fiction.”

In person, you would never take this boyish chatterbox for a zeitgeist-surfing A24 auteur whose fanclub includes Ari Aster, Darren Aronofsky and the Safdie brothers. In fact, you might think twice before serving him alcohol, at least without ID. His mini pompadour gives him an Eraserhead Jr look; his black, round-framed glasses might have been felt-tipped on to his face by a classmate. A black-and-white striped shirt worn under his suit jacket lends him the appearance of a well-dressed humbug.

Though based in fact, Primetime is Oppenheim’s first non-documentary feature. His haunting 2020 debut, Some Kind of Heaven , was set in a Florida retirement community where happiness becomes oppressive and tyrannical. Its 2024 follow-up, Spermworld, delved into the private lives of men who donate sperm, including one who has fathered more than a hundred children.

“I’ve always wanted my documentaries to feel like Hollywood dramas,” the director explains. “With Primetime, I was curious about what it would be like to make an actual Hollywood drama with actors.” The resulting character study is almost as kaleidoscopic and overripe as Ren Faire , Oppenheim’s masterful 2024 HBO “docu-fantasia” featuring a mercurial, Viagra-popping elderly theme-park despot, his back-stabbing underlings and a giant talking lizard.

The film-maker’s own introduction to Chris Hansen came as a child when he saw him spoofed on an episode of South Park, in which Cartman is strong-armed by the presenter into appearing on a TV special about Tourette syndrome; a group of paedophiles inadvertently come to his rescue by shooting themselves en masse. From there, Oppenheim became hooked on To Catch a Predator and its derivatives. A few years ago, his girlfriend (now wife) even bought him a personalised Cameo video message from Hansen. He scoots forward now to play it to me on his phone. In the video, the silver-haired paedophile-hunter cheekily invites Oppenheim to “have a seat … not because I suspect you of anything predator-like,” before plugging his own upcoming shows.

It is this confusion between righteous avenger and meretricious huckster that makes Hansen such an irresistible subject. “I think he started off with noble intentions, but he turned serious reporting into entertainment and willingly transformed himself into a meme. He’s on Cameo presenting what he does as a service you can pay for; then he puts his whole project into this moral register where he talks about good and evil. What happens to you psychologically when you believe you’re doing something good for the world? Does that turn you into a superhero?” He grins: “And now we’ve got the guy who plays Batman as Chris Hansen.”

It was Pattinson, already a diehard Hansen fan, who brought the project to Oppenheim intending only to produce rather than star in it. “Rob’s quite possibly the actor of our time,” the director says. “Every movie he’s done this year has been a defining cultural moment.” Primetime follows The Drama, his prickly black comedy with Zendaya, and The Odyssey; Dune: Part Three arrives in December. “As I’ve gotten to know him, I feel like he also stitched some very human and vulnerable parts of himself into Primetime. Rob became an overnight celebrity when he went to Comic-Con with Twilight in 2008. He was instantly a public figure with expectations about how he should behave. That’s part of what Chris Hansen goes through in the movie.”

The special alchemy of Primetime lies in the way it renders Hansen’s story in the clammy style of To Catch a Predator so that we are simultaneously inside the show, with its churning moral tumult, and outside, looking on in appalled and impotent horror. “It is very much not a biopic,” agrees Oppenheim. “I wanted it to be experiential and phantasmagorical. I was wondering what would happen if you took Billy Wilder’s Ace in the Hole, Oliver Stone’s JFK and Brian De Palma’s Body Double, then threw them in a blender with the real-life events of To Catch a Predator. Would it taste weird or delicious? Maybe you sprinkle a little Sexy Beast in there, too, and it’s, like, ‘Boom!’”

Boom, indeed. Hansen, who has griped bitterly about not being consulted or even informed about the film, has accused Primetime of “weaponised empathy”, “[making] audiences feel sorry for the predators” and portraying him and his staff “as ratings-obsessed, maniacal people”. On the other hand, he has insinuated himself enthusiastically into the Primetime experience, booking trailers for his own true-crime streaming platform, TruBlu, to run immediately before screenings of the movie in US cinemas.

Oppenheim is full of admiration. “The way he has created a media circus around his reaction to the film is on a par with what we’ve seen of him on television. He contains multitudes. He is a journalist but also an entertainer, a circus ringleader and maybe a compulsive performer.” Are there parallels with the current US president? “Well, they were both on television around the same time and both on shows which were made or green-lit by Jeff Zucker, who plays himself in the film.” He stops short, though, of calling them kindred spirits.

Perhaps Hansen’s persona is too closely intertwined with the development of Oppenheim’s own sensibility for him to make any such damning judgment. “I saw To Catch a Predator long before I saw Abbas Kiarostami’s Close-Up or Orson Welles’s F For Fake,” he says, citing two films in which documentary and drama form an unstable concoction. “But I feel the show has a lot in common with them because it’s such a reality bender. It has short adult actors pretending to be children in a house that looks like a set from Blue Velvet.” He shakes his head as if experiencing afresh the insanity of To Catch a Predator. “I don’t think I’d be making nonfiction films the way I do if I hadn’t seen that show as a kid.”

Primetime is in UK cinemas from 30 October. You Can See Everything is in UK cinemas from 20 November

article_text:
Stephen Chow ’s “ Kung Fu Soccer ” will hit cinemas in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and Ireland on Oct. 23, with Singapore-based distributor Encore Films releasing the action-comedy in its original language as well as in a newly produced English-dubbed version.

Jimmy O. Yang, MC Jin and Chow all voice their own characters in English for the dub. A Cantonese-language dub has also been finished, with its voice cast yet to be revealed.

Related Stories

Impulso Morelia: Tatiana Huezo’s ‘Galerna’ Takes Top José María Riba Award, With 'Homeboys' Another Key Winner

Fueled by ‘La Bola Negra,' Spain’s Indie Distribution Make Robust Gains, to Be Highlighted at Valladolid's Merci Market

The North American and U.K. rollout comes after the film’s cinema run in Asia and Oceania. Released in mainland China on July 11, “Kung Fu Soccer” was the country’s top-grossing title of the summer season, earning some $349 million. It then opened across Southeast Asia in August, starting in Singapore and Cambodia on Aug. 6, then Indonesia, Hong Kong, Macao, Malaysia, Brunei and Thailand.

Zhang Xiaofei, Dilraba Dilmurat and Lay Zhang Yixing head the cast, which also includes Carina Lau, Satoh Takeru, Sisley Choi, Angel Woo, Xue Ye, Louis Cheung, Yang and MC Jin. The story centers on the Emei Women’s Football Team, written off as underdogs, as it competes for the Supreme Invincible Cup. Led by captain Shuangshuang, striker Yulong and mentor Xu Feng, the players fuse martial arts technique with ball skills in their push for the title.

The film sees Chow return, 25 years on, to the sports-meets-kung-fu territory he staked out in 2001 with “ Shaolin Soccer ,” which built a global fanbase. He followed it in 2004 with “Kung Fu Hustle,” known for its intricate fight choreography and visual inventiveness. This time, a team of women takes the field.

“Following the tremendous response to ‘Kung Fu Soccer’ across Asia and Oceania, we’re excited to bring the film to cinema audiences in the U.K., Canada, U.K. and Ireland,” said Joyce Lee, managing director of Encore Films.

Lee said Chow’s films had always crossed language and cultural lines, uniting audiences through his mix of action, comedy and heart. “At Encore Films, we believe that great films and the filmmakers behind them deserve more than just a theatrical release. Their creative vision and legacy should be respected, carefully nurtured and developed for generations to come,” she said.

Founded in 2003, Encore has released titles including “Ne Zha 2,” “John Wick: Chapter 4,” “Suzume,” “The Boy and the Heron,” “The New King of Comedy” and “La La Land.” The company is also active in production, with “Young & Fabulous,” a box office success in Singapore, among its credits. Its second feature, “Fat Hope,” is in post-production.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: A big-screen adaptation of David D. Magee’s memoir Dear William : A Father’s Memoir of Addiction, Recovery, Love, and Loss has been greenlit, with production underway in Mississippi, and Andrew Hyatt ( The Blind and Paul ) directing.

Hyatt has also written the film’s screenplay. Matt Passmore, Emily Rose, Gabriel Nagy and Hudson Macready star in the film, which tells the true story of a family confronting addiction and loss while finding its way back to one another. Magee is also producing the film, alongside Cory Pyke.

Passmore plays David, a divorced, broke, and unraveling father who sets out for California with his oldest son, William (Nagy), on a two-thousand-mile drive. Along the way, he discovers that they are both struggling with addiction. The synopsis continues: With Rose portraying Kent and Macready playing Hudson, the story expands beyond father and son to follow a family reckoning with the truths it has kept hidden, navigating marriage, loss, and faith, and discovering the possibility of hope and joy on the other side. At its heart is a son’s final request that gives his father a lifelong purpose.

Passmore is best known for his leading roles as detective Jim Longworth in A&E’s The Glades and Neil Truman in USA Network’s Satisfaction . His additional television credits include McLeod’s Daughters , Frayed, and Netflix’s 13 Reasons Why , while his film work includes Jigsaw .

Rose starred as Audrey Parker in Syfy’s Haven . Her television credits also include Brothers & Sisters , Jericho , and ER . Macready is an actor, singer-songwriter, and guitarist whose screen credits include a recurring role on ABC’s High Potential .

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "O ne man and his dog have an amazing adventure in this survivalist drama starring Brad Pitt, from screenwriter Cameron Alexander and director David Ayer, for which the first and last words of the title have been carefully chosen to signal a mix of sentimentality and thrills. It’s an entertaining anthro-canine-mance, with man and dog relating to each other on a deep level … kind of like Owen Wilson in Marley & Me , only without Jennifer Aniston, or Bernie Winters and Schnorbitz, only without the devastating melancholy.", "links": [{"text": "Owen Wilson in Marley & Me", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2009/mar/13/marley-and-me-film-review"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Pitt, who last worked with Ayer on the second world war action thriller Fury , plays a US military special forces veteran called Belmont, tough, self-reliant and laconically good-humoured in the classic Pitt manner, now spending his retirement roaming the breathtaking remote landscape of Alaska in his seaplane. He is accompanied by his beloved service dog Odin, or Odey (played by four different German shepherds), who saw action with Belmont in various fuzzily imagined flashback combat sequences. Odin took retirement with Belmont and is now his best and only pal. Whether or not Belmont ever had a human partner is never revealed.", "links": [{"text": "second world war action thriller Fury", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2014/oct/23/fury-review-brad-pitt-second-world-war-drama"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Their lives together look heavenly, but a heartstoppingly dramatic event means that Belmont must make an extraordinary journey across rough and hostile terrain, on foot, during which he must look after Odin and Odin must look after him. And the dog is no mere passenger in this ordeal; at one stage Odin gets into a stare-out contest with a digital bear, and a mano-a-mano fight with some digital wolves. Visual effects work, however top-drawer it is, always slightly undermines the feeling of real jeopardy, which here is otherwise expertly maintained. Among the humans they encounter is a grizzled old former goldminer played by JK Simmons (channelling Walter Huston), and Anna Lambe as a young woman who fatefully enters the story at its very beginning.", "links": [{"text": "JK Simmons", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/jk-simmons"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The idea of a man and a dog having no one in this world but each other is an engagingly bittersweet idea; as well as calling up the hardihood of Jack London, it speaks of loneliness and companionship at the same time. Yet weirdly, Belmont is not unlike Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth in Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, living in a trailer all on his own except for his loyal pitbull Brandy, a dog which can go into terrifying attack mode on a prearranged signal. article_text:
O ne man and his dog have an amazing adventure in this survivalist drama starring Brad Pitt, from screenwriter Cameron Alexander and director David Ayer, for which the first and last words of the title have been carefully chosen to signal a mix of sentimentality and thrills. It’s an entertaining anthro-canine-mance, with man and dog relating to each other on a deep level … kind of like Owen Wilson in Marley & Me , only without Jennifer Aniston, or Bernie Winters and Schnorbitz, only without the devastating melancholy.

Pitt, who last worked with Ayer on the second world war action thriller Fury , plays a US military special forces veteran called Belmont, tough, self-reliant and laconically good-humoured in the classic Pitt manner, now spending his retirement roaming the breathtaking remote landscape of Alaska in his seaplane. He is accompanied by his beloved service dog Odin, or Odey (played by four different German shepherds), who saw action with Belmont in various fuzzily imagined flashback combat sequences. Odin took retirement with Belmont and is now his best and only pal. Whether or not Belmont ever had a human partner is never revealed.

Their lives together look heavenly, but a heartstoppingly dramatic event means that Belmont must make an extraordinary journey across rough and hostile terrain, on foot, during which he must look after Odin and Odin must look after him. And the dog is no mere passenger in this ordeal; at one stage Odin gets into a stare-out contest with a digital bear, and a mano-a-mano fight with some digital wolves. Visual effects work, however top-drawer it is, always slightly undermines the feeling of real jeopardy, which here is otherwise expertly maintained. Among the humans they encounter is a grizzled old former goldminer played by JK Simmons (channelling Walter Huston), and Anna Lambe as a young woman who fatefully enters the story at its very beginning.

The idea of a man and a dog having no one in this world but each other is an engagingly bittersweet idea; as well as calling up the hardihood of Jack London, it speaks of loneliness and companionship at the same time. Yet weirdly, Belmont is not unlike Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth in Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, living in a trailer all on his own except for his loyal pitbull Brandy, a dog which can go into terrifying attack mode on a prearranged signal. (Belmont has the same setup with Odin.) Booth and Brandy are Mr Hyde to Belmont and Odin’s Dr Jekyll.

As for Pitt himself, his acting chops are tested when he has to sob and then laugh with joy when it looks wrongly as if Odin has been fatally wounded – but extravagant emoting is not why we love him. Heart of the Beast is a bit cheesy and the final moments will test your credulity, but Pitt is the right guy in the right film.
